# SQS, SNS and EventBridge: say it

<!-- speak:start id=messaging-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** SQS, SNS, EventBridge: all three move messages. When do I use which?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** SQS holds work for one consumer. SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber. EventBridge routes events from AWS services and SaaS apps by content.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: SQS for work, SNS for copies, EventBridge for events.

It works like this. SQS is a queue that consumers poll.

A message stays in the queue until it's processed or it expires.

SNS is a topic that pushes each message to every subscriber, right away.

EventBridge receives events from AWS services and SaaS apps.

A rule matches the event content and sends it to up to five targets.

The thing to watch is that a standard SNS topic doesn't store messages.

So put a queue behind the topic for any consumer that can be down.

In your case, a topic can fan out each finished transcript to a queue per system.

Which of your systems must keep working when another one is down?

**Skeleton.** queue: work at own pace / topic: a copy for everyone / rule: match and route events / queue behind the topic

**Must say.**

- SQS is pull-based: consumers poll the queue, and a message stays in the queue until it is processed or expires.
- SNS is push-based, and a standard topic does not persist messages: it delivers them to subscribers in real time.
- To fan out identical messages, subscribe several SQS queues to one SNS topic; SNS delivers each message to all of them.
- EventBridge rules match events and route them to targets; the default event bus receives events from AWS services automatically.

**Do not say.**

- "SNS stores messages until the subscriber is back.". Say: A standard SNS topic does not persist messages; it delivers them to subscribers in real time. Subscribe an SQS queue to keep each copy.
- "One SQS queue gives every service its own copy.". Say: To fan out identical messages, subscribe one SQS queue per service to an SNS topic. SNS delivers each message to all the subscribed queues.
- "An event bus keeps every event for replay by default.". Say: A Classic event bus, the type with rules and targets, does not retain events. To keep events, add an archive.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Is there a limit on targets for one EventBridge rule? Yes. The maximum number of targets of one rule is 5, and this quota is not adjustable. For more receivers, add a second rule or send to an SNS topic.
- Which one should receive events from our SaaS tools? EventBridge. It is the only event-based service that integrates directly with third-party SaaS partners.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=messaging-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Our worker crashed in the middle of a job. Did we lose that message?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** No. Receiving a message only hides it. If your worker doesn't delete it, the message comes back when the visibility timeout ends.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is no, as long as the worker didn't delete it.

It works like this. When a worker receives a message, the message stays in the queue.

It's only hidden from other consumers for a time.

That hidden time is the visibility timeout. The default is thirty seconds.

If the worker crashes before the delete, the message becomes visible again.

Then the same worker or another one receives it and tries again.

The thing to watch is that the job can now run twice.

So the worker must be idempotent: a second run must do no harm.

Also set the timeout longer than your longest job.

With a redrive policy, a message that keeps failing moves to a dead-letter queue.

In your case, how long does your longest job take?

**Skeleton.** receive hides, delete removes / comes back after the timeout / make the worker idempotent / timeout longer than the job

**Must say.**

- Receiving a message does not delete it: the message stays in the queue, temporarily invisible to other consumers.
- If the consumer does not process and delete the message before the visibility timeout expires, the message becomes visible again and is not lost.
- The default visibility timeout is 30 seconds.
- A standard queue gives at-least-once delivery, so design the consumers to be idempotent.

**Do not say.**

- "The message is gone.". Say: A message that is not processed and deleted before the visibility timeout expires becomes visible again, so it is not lost.
- "SQS delivers each message exactly once.". Say: A standard queue gives at-least-once delivery: more than one copy of a message can be delivered.
- "The dead-letter queue retries the message for you.". Say: Retries happen in the source queue. After maxReceiveCount receives, SQS moves the message to the dead-letter queue.

**Follow-up questions.**

- How long should the visibility timeout be? Longer than the processing time. If it is shorter, another consumer receives a duplicate. If it is far longer, a failed message waits a long time before the next attempt.
- What if one job needs more time than the timeout? The worker can extend the timeout of that message with ChangeMessageVisibility. The maximum is 12 hours from the ReceiveMessage request, and extending does not reset it.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Standard queue or FIFO queue: which should we start with?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Start with a standard queue. Choose FIFO when order per customer, or no duplicates, is a hard rule.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both keep your messages safe. The difference is order and duplicates against throughput.

It works like this. A standard queue scales to a nearly unlimited rate.

But it can deliver a message twice, and the order can change.

A FIFO queue keeps strict order inside each message group.

It doesn't introduce duplicates, but its rate is lower.

Different message groups are processed in parallel.

The thing to watch is that you can't convert a standard queue to FIFO later.

You'd create a new FIFO queue instead.

In your case, start with a standard queue and idempotent workers.

If order per customer matters, use FIFO, with the customer ID as group ID.

Does anything break if one customer's events arrive out of order?

**Skeleton.** order and duplicates against throughput / standard: fast, twice, any order / FIFO: order per group / no conversion later

**Must say.**

- Standard queues support a nearly unlimited number of API calls per second for each action.
- A standard queue gives at-least-once delivery: a message can be delivered more than once, and messages can arrive out of order.
- A FIFO queue keeps strict order within one message group ID and does not introduce duplicates into the queue.
- You cannot convert an existing standard queue into a FIFO queue; you create a new FIFO queue.

**Do not say.**

- "A standard queue keeps the order.". Say: A standard queue makes a best-effort attempt to keep the order. Messages can occasionally arrive out of order.
- "A FIFO queue keeps one order across all customers.". Say: Messages with different message group IDs can arrive or be processed out of order relative to one another.
- "You can switch the queue to FIFO later.". Say: You cannot convert an existing standard queue into a FIFO queue. You create a new FIFO queue.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Is a FIFO queue fast enough for us? By default, a FIFO queue supports 300 messages per second, or 3,000 messages per second with batching. For more, turn on high throughput mode: up to 70,000 transactions per second in some Regions. More message groups give more parallel processing.
- What stops a FIFO queue from delivering the same message twice? Messages with the same deduplication ID sent within a 5 minute deduplication interval are treated as duplicates, and only one copy is delivered.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** On launch day, uploads failed. What did we change so that it cannot happen again?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Each upload now waits safely in a queue instead of failing when the worker is busy. Results reach every system that needs them.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: an upload no longer waits for a busy worker.

It works like this. Each upload now goes into a queue, a waiting list that AWS keeps safe.

Each message is stored in several separate locations before AWS confirms it.

Workers take jobs from the queue at their own pace.

A recording that keeps failing is moved aside, so it blocks no one.

When a transcript is ready, one message reaches both the webhooks and search.

The thing to watch is that processing isn't instant. Customers see a processing status first.

If no worker processes a message, the queue deletes it after four days by default.

In your case, the next step is a warning when a job takes too long.

How long can a customer wait for a transcript before we warn them?

**Skeleton.** uploads wait in a queue / stored in several locations / failing recordings moved aside / not instant: show a status

**Must say.**

- SQS stores each message redundantly in multiple Availability Zones before it acknowledges the send.
- With a queue, components send and receive messages without each component being available at the same time.
- A redrive policy moves a message to a dead-letter queue after the maximum number of receives, so one failing recording blocks no one.
- When a message is published to the topic, SNS sends it to each subscribed queue, so webhooks and search both get every transcript.

**Do not say.**

- "Nothing can ever fail again.". Say: Processing can still fail. A message that is not processed and deleted becomes visible again for another attempt, so it is not lost.
- "Transcripts are ready at once now.". Say: The queue lets components send and receive messages without each being available at the same time, so processing happens later, not at once.
- "We fixed it with more servers.". Say: The fix is the queue between the steps. SQS scales transparently for spikes without any provisioning instructions.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What happens to a recording that keeps failing? After the maximum number of receives, SQS moves it to a dead-letter queue, so it blocks no one. After a fix, a redrive moves it back to the source queue by default.
- Can a message wait in the queue forever? No. A queue keeps a message for 4 days by default. The retention period can be set from 60 seconds to 14 days.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
